name: Chemistry Basics
author: Recurse
subject: science
description: Atoms, the periodic table, bonding, moles, balanced equations, acids and bases, and reaction energy.

lesson.intro: Chemistry is the study of what matter is made of and how it changes. Everything around you is built from about a hundred kinds of atoms. How an atom is put together decides where it sits in the periodic table, how it bonds with other atoms and how it reacts.

sections.title: Inside the atom
sections.body:
An atom has a tiny, dense nucleus at its centre, surrounded by electrons.

- Protons sit in the nucleus and carry a charge of +1. Each has a mass of about 1 atomic mass unit (u).
- Neutrons also sit in the nucleus. They have no charge and about the same mass as a proton.
- Electrons move around the nucleus in shells (energy levels). Each carries a charge of −1 and has about 1/1836 of a proton's mass, so electrons add almost nothing to an atom's mass.

The number of protons is the atomic number, and it defines the element: every atom with 6 protons is carbon, and every atom with 8 is oxygen. The mass number is the number of protons plus neutrons.

Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons. These versions are called isotopes. Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons and carbon-14 has 8, but both are carbon and react in the same way.

A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons. An atom that gains or loses electrons becomes an ion. Losing an electron leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion is positive: sodium becomes Na⁺. Gaining an electron makes a negative ion: chlorine becomes Cl⁻.
sections.code:
Oxygen-16
protons:    8   (atomic number, makes it oxygen)
neutrons:   8   (mass number − atomic number = 16 − 8)
electrons:  8   (neutral atom, same as protons)

O²⁻ ion:    8 protons, 10 electrons, charge −2
sections.tip: Protons decide the element, neutrons decide the isotope, and electrons decide the charge.

check.question: An atom has 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 17 electrons. What is its mass number?
check.explanation: The mass number counts the particles in the nucleus: 17 protons + 18 neutrons = 35. Electrons are not counted because their mass is tiny. With 17 protons, this atom is chlorine-35.

sections.title: The periodic table
sections.body:
The periodic table lists the elements in order of atomic number. Its layout groups together elements that behave alike.

- Rows are called periods. Each step to the right adds one proton and one electron, and each new period starts a new electron shell.
- Columns are called groups. Elements in the same main group (groups 1, 2 and 13 to 18) have the same number of outer-shell electrons, called valence electrons, so they react in similar ways. Helium, with 2, is the one exception in group 18.
- Metals fill the left and middle of the table, nonmetals sit on the upper right, and metalloids such as silicon lie along the staircase line between them.

Each element has a one- or two-letter symbol. Many come from English names (H, C, O), but some come from Latin: Na for sodium (natrium), K for potassium (kalium) and Fe for iron (ferrum).

A few families to know:

- Group 1, the alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium): one valence electron; soft metals that react vigorously with water.
- Group 17, the halogens (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine): seven valence electrons; very reactive nonmetals.
- Group 18, the noble gases (helium, neon, argon): full outer shells, so they barely react at all.

Two trends follow from atomic structure. Atomic radius shrinks from left to right across a period, because each extra proton pulls the same shell in tighter, and it grows down a group, because each row adds a shell. Electronegativity, an atom's pull on shared electrons, does the opposite: it rises across a period and falls down a group. Fluorine is the most electronegative element.
sections.code:
Period 2:     Li   Be   B    C    N    O    F    Ne
Group:        1    2    13   14   15   16   17   18
Valence e⁻:   1    2    3    4    5    6    7    8

Across a period:  radius shrinks, electronegativity rises
Down a group:     radius grows,   electronegativity falls
sections.tip: The group tells you how an element behaves; the period tells you how many electron shells it has.

check.question: Which element is most similar in its chemistry to sodium (Na)?
check.explanation: Potassium is in group 1 with sodium, so it also has one valence electron and reacts in a similar way. Magnesium is sodium's neighbour in the same period, but neighbours along a row behave differently; it is columns, not rows, that share chemistry.

sections.title: Ionic and covalent bonds
sections.body:
Atoms bond because the bonded arrangement is more stable, usually because each atom ends up with a full outer shell. For most atoms that means eight outer electrons (the octet rule); hydrogen needs only two.

Ionic bonding happens between a metal and a nonmetal. The metal gives electrons to the nonmetal, and the resulting positive and negative ions attract each other strongly. In sodium chloride, each sodium atom gives one electron to a chlorine atom, making Na⁺ and Cl⁻. Ionic compounds:

- form a giant crystal lattice of alternating ions rather than separate molecules
- have high melting points (table salt melts at 801 °C)
- conduct electricity when melted or dissolved in water, because the ions can then move, but not as solids

Covalent bonding happens between nonmetals. Instead of transferring electrons, the atoms share pairs of them. In a water molecule, oxygen shares one pair of electrons with each of two hydrogen atoms. Atoms can also share two pairs (a double bond, as in O=C=O, carbon dioxide) or three. Small covalent molecules such as water, carbon dioxide and methane usually have low melting and boiling points and do not conduct electricity.

Sharing is not always equal. Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so in water the shared electrons sit closer to the oxygen. That gives oxygen a slight negative charge and the hydrogens a slight positive charge, making it a polar covalent bond.
sections.code:
Ionic:     Na  +  Cl   →   Na⁺  Cl⁻      (1 electron transferred)
Covalent:  H–O–H                         (2 shared pairs, one per O–H bond)
Double:    O=C=O                         (2 shared pairs per bond)
sections.tip: Metal plus nonmetal: think ionic, electrons transferred. Nonmetal plus nonmetal: think covalent, electrons shared.

check.question: Which pair of elements is most likely to form an ionic compound?
check.explanation: Magnesium is a metal and oxygen is a nonmetal, so magnesium gives two electrons to oxygen, forming Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions. Every other pair is two nonmetals, which share electrons in covalent bonds.

sections.title: The mole and balanced equations
sections.body:
Atoms are far too small to count one by one, so chemists count them in moles. One mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles, a number called Avogadro's number. A mole of carbon atoms, a mole of water molecules and a mole of electrons all contain that many particles.

The mole is chosen so that masses line up with the periodic table. The molar mass of a substance, in grams per mole, equals its relative atomic or formula mass. Carbon's is about 12.0, so one mole of carbon has a mass of 12.0 g. For a compound, add up its atoms: water, H₂O, is 2 × 1.0 + 16.0 = 18.0 g/mol. To convert a mass into moles, divide: moles = mass / molar mass. So 36 g of water is 36 / 18 = 2 mol.

A chemical equation shows reactants turning into products. In a reaction, atoms are rearranged but never created or destroyed, so a balanced equation has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides. To balance one, change the coefficients (the large numbers in front of each formula), never the subscripts. Changing a subscript changes the substance itself: H₂O is water, but H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide.

Hydrogen burning in oxygen, H₂ + O₂ → H₂O, has two oxygen atoms on the left but only one on the right. Putting a 2 in front of H₂O fixes the oxygen but leaves four hydrogen atoms on the right, so put a 2 in front of H₂ as well: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
sections.code:
Counting atoms in  2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O

             left   right
hydrogen      4       4
oxygen        2       2      balanced

moles = mass / molar mass
36 g of H₂O ÷ 18 g/mol = 2 mol
sections.tip: Balance one element at a time, and leave elements that appear on their own, such as O₂, until last.

check.question: Which of these equations for burning methane is balanced?
check.explanation: Count each element: 1 carbon on each side, 4 hydrogens on each side (CH₄ and 2H₂O), and 4 oxygens on each side (2O₂ on the left; 2 in CO₂ plus 2 in 2H₂O on the right). Each of the other options leaves hydrogen or oxygen unbalanced.

sections.title: Reactions: types, energy, acids and bases
sections.body:
Most reactions you will meet fit a few patterns:

- Synthesis: two or more substances combine into one. 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl
- Decomposition: one substance breaks apart. 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂
- Single replacement: an element takes another's place in a compound. Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu
- Double replacement: two compounds swap partners. AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO₃
- Combustion: a fuel burns in oxygen, making carbon dioxide and water. CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O

Every reaction involves energy. Breaking bonds always takes in energy, and forming bonds always gives energy out. If forming the new bonds releases more energy than breaking the old ones took, the reaction is exothermic: it releases heat and its surroundings get warmer, as with burning fuel or a hand warmer. If breaking the bonds takes more energy than forming new ones releases, the reaction is endothermic: it absorbs heat and its surroundings get colder, as in photosynthesis or an instant cold pack.

An acid releases hydrogen ions (H⁺) in water; hydrochloric acid, HCl, is an example. A base accepts H⁺ or releases hydroxide ions (OH⁻); sodium hydroxide, NaOH, is one. The pH scale, which usually runs from 0 to 14, measures how acidic a solution is:

- pH 7 is neutral, like pure water at 25 °C.
- Below 7 is acidic: lemon juice is about pH 2.
- Above 7 is basic (alkaline): household bleach is around pH 12.

The scale is logarithmic: each step of 1 is a factor of 10 in H⁺ concentration. A solution at pH 3 has ten times the H⁺ concentration of one at pH 4, and a hundred times that of one at pH 5.

When an acid and a base react, they neutralize each other, forming a salt and water: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.
sections.code:
Exothermic:   releases heat, surroundings warm up    (burning, hand warmers)
Endothermic:  absorbs heat, surroundings cool down   (photosynthesis, cold packs)

pH  0 ........ 7 ........ 14
    acidic   neutral   basic
Each step of 1 = 10 times the H⁺ concentration
sections.tip: Breaking bonds always costs energy. A reaction gives out energy only because the new bonds it forms release more than that.

check.question: Heating limestone drives the reaction CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. What type of reaction is it?
check.explanation: One compound breaks down into two simpler substances, which is decomposition. Synthesis is the reverse, where substances combine into one, and combustion needs a fuel reacting with oxygen.

keyTerms.definition: The number of protons in an atom's nucleus. It defines which element the atom is.
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, such as carbon-12 and carbon-14.
An atom or group of atoms with an electric charge because it has gained or lost electrons.
Electrons in the outermost shell. They take part in bonding and set an element's chemistry.
A bond in which two atoms share a pair of electrons, typically between nonmetals.
An amount of substance containing 6.022 × 10²³ particles.
A scale of acidity: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral and above 7 is basic. Each unit is a factor of 10.
Describes a reaction that releases energy, usually as heat, to its surroundings.

summary: Protons set the element, neutrons set the isotope, and electrons set the charge.
Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, so they behave alike; atoms shrink across a period and grow down a group.
Metals and nonmetals form ionic bonds by transferring electrons; nonmetals form covalent bonds by sharing them.
moles = mass / molar mass, and a balanced equation conserves atoms: change coefficients, never subscripts.
Breaking bonds absorbs energy and forming bonds releases it; pH below 7 is acidic, and each pH step is a factor of 10.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why table salt forms hard crystals and conducts electricity when dissolved, while sugar dissolves without conducting, using what you know about ionic and covalent bonds.

questions.question: What determines which element an atom is?
questions.explanation: The atomic number, the count of protons, defines the element. Changing the number of neutrons gives a different isotope of the same element, and changing the number of electrons gives an ion, but neither changes the element.

questions.question: How many neutrons are in an atom of iron-56? Iron's atomic number is 26.
questions.explanation: Mass number = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = 56 − 26 = 30. The atomic number gives the protons, and the number in the isotope's name is the mass number.

questions.question: A sodium atom turns into a sodium ion, Na⁺. What happened?
questions.explanation: Losing one negative electron leaves 11 protons and 10 electrons, so the ion has a +1 charge. Gaining a proton is the tempting answer, but protons never change in a chemical reaction; if they did, the atom would become a different element.

questions.question: Moving from sodium to argon across period 3, what happens to the size of the atoms?
questions.explanation: Each step adds a proton, while the new electrons go into the same outer shell. The stronger pull of the nucleus draws that shell in, so atoms shrink across a period. It is tempting to think more particles means a bigger atom, but size only jumps when a new shell starts in the next period.

questions.question: Why are noble gases such as neon and argon so unreactive?
choices: Their atoms are too heavy to move
Their outer electron shells are already full
questions.explanation: A full outer shell is already stable, so noble gas atoms gain nothing by gaining, losing or sharing electrons. They do have electrons and neutrons; argon, for example, has 18 electrons and 22 neutrons in its most common isotope.

questions.question: What is the chemical symbol for potassium?
questions.explanation: Potassium's symbol, K, comes from its Latin name, kalium. P is phosphorus and Po is polonium, so guessing from the English name does not work for this element.

questions.question: Compare ionic and covalent bonding: which kinds of elements form each, and what happens to the electrons?
questions.answer: Ionic bonds form between a metal and a nonmetal: the metal transfers electrons to the nonmetal, and the oppositely charged ions attract. Covalent bonds form between nonmetals, which share pairs of electrons.
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride (NaCl) is ionic; water (H₂O) and methane (CH₄) are covalent. The bond type explains properties: ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct when dissolved, while small covalent molecules usually do neither.

questions.question: Solid table salt does not conduct electricity, but salt dissolved in water does. Why?
choices: Dissolved ions are free to move and carry charge
Water supplies free electrons to the salt
Dissolving turns the ionic bonds into covalent bonds
Solid salt contains no charged particles
questions.explanation: Salt is made of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in both forms. In the solid they are locked in place in a lattice; in water they separate and move, so they can carry a current. Solid salt is full of charged particles; they just cannot move.

questions.question: What is the molar mass of carbon dioxide, CO₂, in g/mol? Use C = 12 and O = 16.
questions.explanation: Add up the atoms: one carbon and two oxygens, 12 + 2 × 16 = 44 g/mol. A common slip is to count oxygen only once and get 28.

questions.question: How many moles are in 90 g of water? The molar mass of water is 18 g/mol.
questions.explanation: moles = mass / molar mass = 90 / 18 = 5 mol. A quick sanity check: 90 g is several times 18 g, so the answer must be several moles, not a fraction of a mole or a huge number.

questions.question: Fill in the missing coefficient to balance the equation: N₂ + 3H₂ → ? NH₃
questions.explanation: The left side has 2 nitrogen atoms and 6 hydrogen atoms. Two molecules of NH₃ also contain 2 nitrogens and 6 hydrogens, so 2 balances both elements: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.

questions.question: A student balances Na + Cl₂ → NaCl by rewriting it as Na + Cl₂ → NaCl₂. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing, because both sides now have two chlorine atoms
Changing a subscript makes a different formula; it should be 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl
Chlorine should be written as Cl, not Cl₂
The sodium should be changed to Na₂ instead
questions.explanation: Subscripts are part of a substance's identity. Sodium chloride is always NaCl, so balancing must use coefficients: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl has 2 sodium and 2 chlorine atoms on each side. Writing chlorine as Cl is also wrong, because chlorine gas exists as Cl₂ molecules.

questions.question: Vinegar has a pH of about 3, and pure water has a pH of 7. How many times greater is the H⁺ concentration in vinegar?
questions.explanation: The pH scale is logarithmic, so each step is a factor of 10. A difference of 4 steps is 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 10,000. Treating the scale as linear and answering 4 is the most common mistake.

questions.question: As a reaction runs, its beaker gets noticeably warmer. What does this tell you?
choices: It is exothermic, releasing energy to the surroundings
Bonds are breaking but none are forming
questions.explanation: A reaction that warms its surroundings is giving out energy, so it is exothermic. An endothermic reaction absorbs heat from its surroundings, so the beaker would feel cold instead.

questions.question: Which statement about chemical bonds and energy is correct?
choices: Breaking bonds releases energy, and forming bonds absorbs it
Both breaking and forming bonds release energy
Breaking and forming bonds involve no energy change
Breaking bonds absorbs energy, and forming bonds releases it
questions.explanation: Pulling bonded atoms apart always takes energy, and atoms give out energy when they bond. A reaction is exothermic overall only when its new bonds release more energy than breaking the old ones took. The idea that breaking bonds releases energy, often heard about fuels and food, is a common misconception.

questions.question: What type of reaction is Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂?
questions.explanation: Zinc, an element, takes the place of hydrogen in HCl, pushing the hydrogen out as H₂ gas. Swapping one element for another in a compound is single replacement. It is not synthesis, because two products form rather than one.

questions.question: What happens when an acid reacts with a base? Give an example.
questions.answer: The acid and base neutralize each other, forming a salt and water: H⁺ from the acid and OH⁻ from the base combine to make H₂O. For example, HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.
questions.explanation: Neutralization is why antacid tablets, which are mild bases, relieve excess stomach acid. When a strong acid and a strong base react in exactly matching amounts, the resulting solution is neutral, at pH 7.
